strengths: The paper contributes a useful resource for conversational NLP: 20,281 preference pairs derived from naturally occurring user feedback, with explicit preference summaries and additional on-policy variants. Connecting feedback extraction, response generation, and preference training is practically valuable.

The complete pipeline has meaningful empirical support across three model families and three established benchmarks. For example, Phi-3 trained on WF GPT-4 improves from 24.3% to 34.9% on AlpacaEval 2 length-controlled win rate and from 15.4% to 32.4% on Arena-Hard. These results support utility beyond the proposed checklist evaluation.

The authors conduct human audits of feedback classification on 50 conversations containing over 500 utterances and checklist evaluation on 200 conversations. Reporting annotator agreement and explicitly separating training and test conversations and users are valuable methodological safeguards.

The framework is generally clearly described, with a dataset link, detailed annotation rubrics and prompts, model identifiers, and key SFT/DPO hyperparameters. The resource and demonstrated training utility support a Findings recommendation, although the stronger attribution and evaluation claims remain insufficiently established for a clear main-conference recommendation.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of authentic feedback. WildFeedback and the regenerated UltraFeedback baselines differ in prompt distribution, conversational context, response construction, and filtering. In the expert setting, newly generated preferred responses are also compared against historical responses. A control using the same WildChat prompts and generation procedure with feedback removed or shuffled would help distinguish feedback-specific benefits from general data and teacher effects. Closely related natural-feedback learning methods are cited but not experimentally compared.

The claim that checklist evaluation more accurately reflects actual user preferences is only partially validated. GPT-4 extracts the preferences, generates expert responses, filters on-policy pairs, and judges the custom evaluation. Increased preference for checklist-conditioned responses after giving the judge that checklist does not independently establish greater validity. Appendix C reports 57.14% GPT-human agreement and kappa 0.372, versus 63.27% and 0.436 between humans. This audit is useful, but it does not compare human agreement with and without checklists or independently validate the extracted summaries against raw feedback.

The custom test set has a deliberately restricted evaluation target: the authors select preferences most similar to others within 70 clusters, producing 540 examples. This is compatible with studying common preferences, but clustering alone does not establish population-majority representativeness. DSAT recall of 48.4%, despite 83.3% precision, further limits feedback coverage. Consequently, claims about diverse or evolving user needs and reduced bias exceed the evidence.

The claims of significant and consistent superiority over UltraFeedback need qualification. Table 3 contains counterexamples: Qwen-2 WF GPT-4 scores below UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate, 39.4% versus 40.6%, and MT-Bench, 7.60 versus 7.66. Several other advantages are small, and no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variation across training runs are reported.

Exact reconstruction is less well specified than the core training recipe. The manuscript omits the clustering embedding model, deduplication thresholds, operational procedure for grouping users, and validation criterion used during hyperparameter search. These details matter because test-set selection is specialized and Appendix D emphasizes sensitivity to training settings.
